other-interests-1f71cad1a5.headline: FAA grounds all U.S. flights days after expanding its AI air traffic system
other-interests-1f71cad1a5.fulltext:
On a typical Friday November evening, millions of passengers would be hopping on flights for pre-Thanksgiving weekend trips and journeys home after work. But today on November 13, domestic and international flights throughout the U.S. completely ground to a halt at about 4 P.M. EST.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) cited a “temporary telecommunications outage,” in a post on X, and all flights have been grounded “out of an abundance of caution.”
The sweeping aviation disruption comes three days after the FAA expanded its Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system, known as SMART. The FAA previously tested the system in the National Capital Region, the airspace around Washington, D.C., in September. The artificial intelligence-driven system is intended to synthesize data on weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics in order to “reduce delays and cancellations,” according to the FAA’s description. As of November 10, it was deployed across all 22 air traffic regions in the country.
On supporting science journalism

Such nationwide groundings are exceedingly rare. The last time the FAA stopped flights was for 90 minutes on January 11, 2023, to address an outage in its Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system, which informs pilots and operators about potential safety hazards. Before that, flights were halted immediately following the September 11, 2001 terror attacks.
The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure is managed by L3Harris, a Silicon Valley-based aerospace and defense company and a contractor for federal government agencies. L3Harris did not immediately respond to Scientific American’s requests for comment. The FAA issued a brief statement, saying that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates.”
Ruth Stilwell, a former air traffic controller and aerospace policy expert, speculates that the outage may be due to a software problem, such as a software update gone awry in the Voice Switching and Control System, which manages communications between pilots and air traffic controllers. It is not Microsoft software, Stilwell emphasizes, referring to the widespread Microsoft product outage that occurred on Thursday into Friday. CBS News reported that a software update to the private communications system may have triggered a system-wide reboot, causing it to crash.
“It would be unusual for them to do a software update during the day, but the FAA is very short-staffed,” Stilwell says. Department of Government Efficiency-related cuts laid off hundreds of FAA workers last year.
"This is yet another example of how brittle our air transportation system is in our country," says Missy Cummings, at George Mason University and a former fighter pilot whose research focuses on responsible AI in transportation. "This has been a problem over several administration, and the Trump administration made the situation much worse with all their cuts."
Even if the problem, software-related or otherwise, was small in scale, it’s standard procedure to ground planes while attempting to communicate through other channels with pilots who have already taken off, Stilwell says.
“The ground stop was the right thing to do,” Stilwell says. “Planes in the air are the top priority. The safety of those flights is way more important than anybody’s delay. The planes on the ground are safe.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.

ai-3dc626ea28.headline: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models — uh-oh, Jensen!
ai-3dc626ea28.fulltext:
The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims.
The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service.
While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang.
U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff.
Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips.
White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination.
That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025.
However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed.
“If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer.
Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and Singaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai.
In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “China problem” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips.
Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry.
If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import.
Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips.
For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate.
The U.S. government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials.

beyond-your-beat-d401914b33.headline: Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI model: Know features, price, and more
beyond-your-beat-d401914b33.fulltext:
Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI model: Know features, price, and more
Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen focuses on faster coding, research and AI agent workflows, with a 1 million-token context window, new safety features, and availability across consumer and developer tools
Listen to This Article
Google has introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, an artificial intelligence (AI) model designed to handle everyday tasks such as coding, research, data analysis and writing. The model focuses on speed and efficiency, particularly for tasks involving multiple steps, reducing the need for users to provide repeated instructions.
Unlike Google's Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon models, which are built for complex reasoning and longer tasks, Hydrogen is designed for faster execution across a wider range of applications. According to Google, the model is aimed at both developers and consumers and is being rolled out across the Gemini app, Google Search, Google AI Studio, the Gemini API and its enterprise services.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen: What’s new
Gemini 4 Hydrogen is designed to carry out tasks that involve multiple steps, particularly those related to software development, research and data processing. It can understand instructions, break down tasks, use external tools and work towards completing a task with limited human intervention.
Google's Gemini 4 lineup includes three models with different roles. Carbon and Argon are designed for complex reasoning, including architectural decisions, analysing difficult problems and handling tasks that require extended planning. Hydrogen, meanwhile, focuses on speed and execution.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen supports a context window of up to one-million tokens. A context window determines how much information an AI model can process and refer to during a conversation or task. This allows Hydrogen to work with large documents, code repositories and other information without having to process everything in smaller, separate sections. 
Also Read
Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Coding and AI workflows
One of the main applications of Hydrogen is software development. Developers can use the model to identify errors, debug existing code, make changes to software projects, run tests and navigate large code repositories.
Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at its default high setting. It also scored 57 per cent on Terminal-Bench 4.1, compared with 18.2 per cent for Gemini 3.8 Flash. Terminal-Bench evaluates how well AI models perform tasks using command-line tools.
The model is also designed to make changes to specific parts of a codebase rather than rewriting entire files. It can read and search multiple files simultaneously, helping developers work with large software projects more efficiently.
Google is also introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity to support workflows involving multiple AI models. Instead of using one model for an entire task, Orchestrator can switch between Carbon and Hydrogen depending on the complexity of the work.
For instance, Carbon can take charge of planning and coordinating a project, while Hydrogen can handle execution, testing and verification. Multiple Hydrogen-powered agents can also work on different parts of a project simultaneously.
On the Terminal-Bench 4.0 evaluation, Google says Orchestrator achieved task success rates close to those of Carbon while consuming 24 per cent less quota on average and completing tasks 19 per cent faster.
Beyond software development, Hydrogen can also handle multi-step activities such as deep research, data analysis and navigating large sets of information. It can process PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio files and recorded videos to prepare reports and structured outputs.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Safeguards
Google says Hydrogen incorporates safety and security improvements from its latest Gemini 4 safety framework. These safeguards are intended to prevent AI agents from taking actions beyond their permissions, following malicious instructions or completing tasks in unintended ways.
The model is also designed to be more resistant to indirect prompt injection attacks, says Google. These attacks involve hiding malicious instructions in external content, such as websites or documents, which an AI agent may access while carrying out a task.
Google says Hydrogen is more than 2.3 times more resilient on the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark. It has also been tested for situations in which a task cannot be completed because of missing information, restricted access or other limitations.
The company says the model is less likely to bypass permission boundaries in such situations and has achieved a 96.7 per cent honesty rate on its internal agent honesty evaluation.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Pricing
For developers accessing the model through the Gemini API, Google has set the price at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.
Input tokens refer to the information provided to the model, including prompts and uploaded content, while output tokens refer to the responses generated by it. Google says the pricing remains the same across the model's one-million token context window.
The model is being made available across different Google products, although access and subscription requirements vary depending on the service being used.
For consumers, the model is available through the model selection menu in the Gemini app. It is also being integrated into Google Search for users globally.
Developers can access Hydrogen through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio and Android Studio. Paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can also use the model through Google Antigravity.

indian-startups-21e94d425e.headline: MeitY Reviews Quick Help Platforms’ Data Collection Process For Physical AI Training
indian-startups-21e94d425e.fulltext: The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sought details from home services platforms, including Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company’s InstaHelp, over the collection of first-person video and sensor data from gig workers for training physical AI models. As per a report by ET , a meeting chaired by MeitY secretary S Krishnan yesterday brought together senior executives from the quick home services platforms and other technology and robotics companies to discuss concerns around workers’ consent, consumer privacy and data sovereignty. Officials are concerned that recordings of everyday household activities could infringe workers’ rights, compromise consumer privacy and pose risks to national data security. The ministry sought details on the standard operating procedures (SOPs) followed by companies for collecting, processing and storing such data. It also sought information on safeguards for obtaining workers’ consent and protecting the privacy of other individuals captured in the recordings. The ministry also sought clarity on whether companies were selling, sharing or transferring the collected data to physical AI developers outside India. It asked Pronto to submit details of its data collection practices and the SOPs it follows, ET reported, citing people familiar with the discussions. When asked by Inc42 about the meeting and the details sought by the ministry, Pronto said it had participated in the meeting as part of a broader industry consultation involving home services platforms, robotics companies and other stakeholders. The spokesperson said that the consultation provided an opportunity for the ministry and industry participants to exchange perspectives, share existing practices and discuss the opportunities and challenges emerging from the evolving AI landscape. “Pronto shared its current practices as part of this exchange and looks forward to continued engagement with MeitY and other industry stakeholders,” the startup said. Inc42 has reached out to Snabbit and Urban Company for their comments on the development. The story will be updated upon receiving responses. Concerns were also reportedly raised about India becoming a source of cheap training data for foreign AI companies. Executives suggested that the country should focus on developing its own physical AI capabilities rather than merely supplying data to overseas developers. This comes shortly after Pronto faced scrutiny over a pilot programme to record household chores using cameras worn by service professionals to generate training data for robotics systems. The controversy also brought Snabbit and Urban Company under scrutiny over their potential involvement in this. Snabbit subsequently clarified that it had conducted a limited assessment of the tech in a controlled training-centre environment but decided against proceeding with the proposal. Urban Company founder Abhiraj Singh Bhal said the company neither records inside customers’ homes nor plans to do so. Pronto, meanwhile, confirmed that it was running an opt-in pilot involving first-person video recordings of household chores. Initially, it said the feature was available only to customers who actively opted in during booking and was limited to less than 0.01% of its users. The startup later told Inc42 that raw footage was deleted immediately after the work was completed, while an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording remained accessible only to customers for 48 hours. The anonymised footage was subsequently used for AI training, as outlined in its terms. This further casts a shadow on Pronto founder Anjali Sardana's expanding ambitions in physical AI beyond the home services business. In July, the startup formalised its data collection experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which professionals wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits. Last month, Sardana launched Provision Labs, a San Francisco-based physical AI venture that will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. Provision Labs also announced the acquisition of Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a startup focused on perception technologies. Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision’s hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models. The relationship between Pronto’s household data collection and Provision Labs’ operations remains unclear.

indian-startups-1bd72439b4.headline: [Update] Razorpay Gets SEBI Nod For ₹6,000 Cr IPO
indian-startups-1bd72439b4.fulltext: Update | November 14, 2026; 01:25 AM IST Fintech major Razorpay has received Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (SEBI) nod to float its proposed initial public offering (IPO). According to SEBI’s latest processing status update, the regulator issued its observations on Razorpay’s draft IPO papers on November 3. In SEBI’s parlance, issuance of observations allows a company to proceed with its public issue. This comes a couple of weeks after Inc42 reported that SEBI had given its go-ahead to the fintech giant to list on the bourses. At the time, sources had said that the ₹5,000 Cr to ₹6,000 Cr ($530 Mn to $630 Mn) IPO would value the company at around $5 Bn (₹47,000 Cr), with a listing likely between January and March 2027. Original | November 4, 2026; 11:08 AM IST Fintech major Razorpay has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed ₹5,000-6,000 Cr IPO, sources told Inc42. The offering is expected to value the company at around $5 Bn, with a listing likely between January and March 2027, the sources added. The IPO is expected to comprise a fresh issue and an offer-for-sale (OFS). However, the proposed split could not be ascertained. The Economic Times first reported the development. Founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, Razorpay offers payment processing, business banking, payroll, and lending solutions. It filed its IPO papers through the confidential route in June, targeting a valuation of $5 Bn to $6 Bn, below the $7.5 Bn valuation it commanded in its last funding round in 2021. Ahead of the listing, Razorpay shifted its domicile from the US to India. The company slipped into the red in FY25, weighed down by ₹1,209 Cr in ESOP expenses and one-time restructuring and tax costs linked to the move. Operating revenue rose 65% to ₹3,783 Cr during the year. Razorpay’s Growing AI Offerings Alongside its IPO preparations, Razorpay has been expanding its AI offerings across payments, marketing, and business operations. Last month, it announced an expanded partnership with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT. Under the partnership, its growth marketing platform, Razorpay Engage, will enable brands to prepare product catalogues and launch and manage campaigns on ChatGPT Ads. Razorpay has also launched Vulcan, a transformer-based AI foundation model for digital payments. The company claims the model can improve payment reliability and safety by scoring payment routes in real time and identifying fraud patterns across multiple merchants once deployed. Built using NVIDIA and AWS technology, Vulcan combines Razorpay’s payments data with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AWS’ cloud infrastructure. The fintech major has also been developing Agent Studio, a platform for deploying task-specific AI agents for businesses. Around 200 businesses were using the platform in beta as of August, with use cases spanning reconciliation, abandoned-cart recovery, subscription recovery, and finance operations. Razorpay has raised over $800 Mn to date from investors including Y Combinator, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed.

world-388c180a1a.headline: Microsoft outage: company scrambles to fix global issue that took down Outlook and Teams
world-388c180a1a.fulltext:
Microsoft has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.
The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.
The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began Thursday evening, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover just before midday GMT on Friday. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.
Earlier on Friday, it said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels” as it brought back services. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use Copilot, Microsoft’s AI chatbot, according to the company.
On Friday, government agencies worldwide, from municipalities in France to the US House of Representatives, reported problems with Microsoft services. The issues were patchy, with some but not all users reporting problems with services including Microsoft Teams and Outlook email.
The outage website Down Detector showed an increase in Microsoft 365 problems at about 6pm GMT on Thursday, with nearly 130,000 reports of problems in 74 countries affecting access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams as well as enterprise services such as SharePoint and OneDrive. Copilot was also affected.
Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.
Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”
The Microsoft outage also hit connectors used by OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI services.
OpenAI said it was investigating a problem with Microsoft connectors in which new connections might be broken and tools were not working as expected. Anthropic said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider affecting its Microsoft 365 connector.
The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.
In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.
Some schools in the UK notified parents that reporting attendance or absence issues had to be done via phone. National Rail, which provides information across the UK network, warned people might not be able to access tickets that had been emailed to them.
US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.
Multiple cities, including the City of Tampa, Florida, posted notices on their municipal websites to say that they were affected by the outage. Law enforcement offices across the US were also affected, with one sheriff’s county in Colorado saying it was unable to process bond payments because Outlook email was down, and requesting that anyone who needed to post bond do so in person.
When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.
In Australia, the financial impact of the outage was expected to cost billions of dollars, according to the risk advisory firm, RSM Australia. Several government agencies, including national security sevices, were unable to access or send emails.
Hospitals and health clinics were affected, although the Australian Medical Association on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care. Courts and schools also struggled to operate as normal.
The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies said fund management services had been disrupted.
In financial markets some portfolio managers have been unable to check emails, making it hard to access on some trading platforms.
In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.
Microsoft last month reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that affected a suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.
Mark Gregory, an associate professor in the School of Engineering at RMIT University in Melbourne, said the outage appeared to be affecting the network layer in Microsoft’s systems, and was potentially similar to the configuration issue that brought down Optus’s network in 2023.
He said that when some of the servers had configuration issues, it meant customers were forced to share a smaller pool of servers to access the cloud services.
“If you lose part of that pool, then all of the users are trying to access the remaining servers, and that overloads them. And then they go down. And so you end up with a cascading problem. Then it takes time to find the underlying problem, in this case, a misconfiguration in the network layer.”
Gregory said businesses reliant on cloud services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options.
Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report

ai-ec577d4c46.headline: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
ai-ec577d4c46.fulltext:
It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.
Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.
Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.
“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”
Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.
“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”
It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.
If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.
Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.
While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.
Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.
Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.
Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.
The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.
OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.
"Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.
ChatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts.
Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kick-start a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents.
OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an "Instant Checkout" feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products.
Nayak said ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI's previous efforts, particularly around product discovery.
"We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they're really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint," she said.
ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old. The limited rollout is intentional, and the "right approach to make sure things are working," said Luke Gebb, executive vice president and global head of innovation at Amex.
OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter. With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to.
"It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there," Gebb told CNBC in an interview.
Merchants and vendors are still reckoning with the rise of personal AI agents, and some companies have opted to forgo them entirely. United Airlines said Wednesday that it will block agents from accessing its systems to book tickets, and Amazon prevents the agents from purchasing products on its platform.
OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition. The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance.
"It's going to take time for the ecosystem to build the right infrastructure to be able to make this experience really amazing and seamless across all of their sites," Nayak said. "Really, who we are speaking to here is the networks and the merchants."

The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, is facing growing pressure over his apparent lack of action over the Nvidia spying scandal as other Trump administration officials publicly raise questions over his decisions.
Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by the company’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, after reports emerged of his multiple affairs, most importantly with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be fired, the Associated Press reported, after it emerged that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration.
Lutnick is now scheduled to testify before Congress next month, just days after the ousted Nvidia chief answers lawmakers’ questions on Capitol Hill.
Lutnick is also facing criticism for a delay by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration.
Bessent has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”, Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added in an interview with the network on Friday.
John Curtis, a Utah Republican senator, said that Lutnick’s reported delay on export controls regarding Megaspeed “raises the question of whether the commerce department is acting in the best interests of the American people”.
The Republican senator John Cornyn told the Financial Times that there needed to be “a thorough investigation and accountability for the outrageous circumvention of national security export controls”, adding: “Heads should roll.”
The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said Jensen Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether US security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about his reported relationship with Alice Huang.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.
Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge. The president called him two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported.
On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”
The House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.
Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair, said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him, citing “recent reports [that] raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology”.
The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal-conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to his “profound” contributions to the company he cofounded.
Huang is reported to have had relationships with Alice Huang as well as an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, according to the New York Times, and another, unnamed employee, according to Reuters.
The House foreign affairs chair, Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Huang’s testimony.
The House speaker, Mike Johnson, said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China.
Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company important to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.
“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters at the US Capitol, adding that he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“
Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models.
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday.
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as Huang’s swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for more than three decades.
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo.
Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.

deep-tech-75520ce395.headline: Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots
deep-tech-75520ce395.fulltext:
OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams.
The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune.  A company spokesperson said that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it.
OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman.
The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen. 
OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022.
OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI. OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. 
The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world.
The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots.
Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks.
Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, reacted to the change at OpenAI, telling Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence—similar to the way the same underlying frontier AI models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work.
OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works.
But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAI to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general AI models.
The reorganization also comes at a time when OpenAI is under pressure to rein in its costs and show that it is more focused on a few, core products. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts—including Sora—in order to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses—which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter—as it seeks to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027.
This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own.
But Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: Their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Such “deployment” experience—and the data these robots gather—helps robots adapt to specific workplaces and tasks. Better foundational models make that site-specific data more valuable because robots can learn from it faster, Tedrake said.
Recent experiments have tested how much work a general-purpose model can do without specialized training on robotic data. Researchers gave Astra camera images, robot information and a control interface that allowed the model to command the robot to take certain actions. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark—where the model commands a simulated robot in a digital simulation, as opposed to a real robot—compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard.
Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. They can cope when a bottle is in a different position or the lighting changes, and reason about the sequence of a task or which step went wrong, he said.
Meanwhile, large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection.
“There may be different starting points for how to grow intelligence,” Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune. He said it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run.
For its part, OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots. 
Back at booth #208 at CoRL, a few former members of the once-unified, stand-alone OpenAI robotics team milled about. They still drew a crowd, despite having no display or demo. After all, one of the conference’s hottest questions was how much robotics expertise would remain valuable as general-purpose models grew more capable—and the experience of those former OpenAI robotics researchers, now dispatched to other teams, offered one answer. 
Update, Nov. 13: This story has been updated to clarify the status of the OpenAI robotics team members who were at CoRL.

climate-energy-758159779a.headline: Why India's black mass export ban matters for its EV battery ambitions
climate-energy-758159779a.fulltext:
Why India's black mass export ban matters for its EV battery ambitions
India's black mass export ban aims to keep valuable battery minerals within the country, support domestic recycling and reduce reliance on imported raw materials for EV manufacturing
Listen to This Article
Earlier this week, the Centre banned the export of waste and scrap from primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators, including black mass recovered from lithium-ion batteries. The restriction has come into force with immediate effect as the government looks to expand domestic battery recycling and strengthen the supply of critical minerals.
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Ministry of Commerce, revised the export policy for the material covered under ITC (HS) Code 85491400, changing its status from 'Free' to 'Prohibited'. The restriction will remain in place until further orders.
The decision is expected to improve the availability of raw materials for domestic recyclers, allowing them to recover valuable minerals and supply them to sectors such as electric vehicles (EVs), battery manufacturing and energy storage.
Why black mass matters for India's EV industry
Black mass is a powder-like material produced by shredding used lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste. It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are used in battery manufacturing.
These minerals are important for India's EV industry as they form part of the battery supply chain. Recovering them from discarded batteries can provide an additional source of raw material for battery makers and reduce the need to depend on imports.
Also Read
India remains substantially dependent on imports for several critical minerals. According to NITI Aayog's September 2026 Trade Watch report, the country is 100 per cent import-dependent for lithium, nickel and cobalt.
The export ban is intended to retain domestically generated black mass so that these minerals can be recovered and reused locally. ALSO READ: Govt bans lithium-ion battery black mass exports to aid domestic recyclers 
What is India's domestic battery recycling capacity
India's battery recycling industry has expanded, but its capacity to process used lithium-ion batteries and recover critical minerals remains limited.
A Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change document, based on discussions held in January 2025, said 16 units in India were processing lithium-ion batteries. Of these, 12 units registered on the Central Pollution Control Board's (CPCB) extended producer responsibility (EPR) portal were also processing black mass to recover metal compounds. Their combined input capacity was 75,500 tonnes a year.
The government has also acknowledged that domestic recycling capacity is not being fully utilised because of inadequate availability of feedstock, or the waste material required for processing.
This leaves recycling facilities with more processing capacity than the available supply of battery waste can support.
What it means for domestic recyclers
The export prohibition is expected to improve the availability of black mass for domestic recycling and refining companies.
In its statement, the Department of Commerce said some Indian recyclers had been importing black mass to meet their requirements even as domestically generated material was being sent overseas.
In a post on LinkedIn, Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) founder Ajay Srivastava said India had more capacity to process black mass than it generated, leaving refiners short of raw material. He said recovering more critical minerals within the country could reduce battery makers' reliance on imports.
Srivastava also pointed to the need for effective enforcement. He said exporters could potentially avoid scrutiny by declaring black mass as cobalt powder, nickel intermediates or other industrial products.
Government push to boost domestic recycling
The export ban is part of the government's wider efforts to strengthen India's critical mineral supply chain.
In September 2025, the Union Cabinet approved a ₹1,500-crore incentive scheme under the National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM) to promote the recovery of critical minerals from secondary sources. These include lithium-ion battery scrap, electronic waste and industrial scrap.
The scheme is expected to support the development of at least 270 kilo tonnes of annual recycling capacity, produce around 40 kilo tonnes of critical minerals annually, attract investments of about ₹8,000 crore and create nearly 70,000 direct and indirect jobs.
In April 2026, the Ministry of Mines said 58 companies had been found eligible to participate in the scheme. These companies had proposed a combined capacity of around 850 kilo tonnes and investments of approximately ₹5,000 crore. These are pledged figures and do not represent operational or commissioned capacity, the ministry said.
The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, also provide a regulatory framework for the sector. Under the rules, battery producers, including importers, must meet annual extended producer responsibility (EPR) targets for the collection and recycling or refurbishment of waste batteries.
The rules also require producers to use minimum quantities of domestically recycled materials in new batteries from FY28 onwards, according to the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.
Together, these measures aim to build a domestic ecosystem for collecting battery waste, recovering critical minerals and supplying them back to manufacturers.
What challenges remain
Despite the expected benefits of the export restriction, India's battery recycling industry continues to face operational and technological hurdles.
Prassann Daphal, chief executive officer (CEO) at e-waste and lithium-ion battery recycler Recyclekaro, told Business Standard that one of the biggest concerns was the collection of used batteries. A large share of battery waste still moves through the informal sector, making it difficult for organised recyclers to secure a steady supply.
He said the industry also faced challenges in recovering battery-grade materials and making the process commercially viable.
"The second is technology and capital. Pulling battery-grade lithium, nickel and cobalt out of black mass through hydrometallurgy is complex and capital-intensive, and it has to run at scale to pay off. The economics also keep shifting. As the market moves towards LFP chemistries, which contain little nickel or cobalt, the value per tonne of feedstock falls," Daphal said.
Another concern, he said, is the limited number of domestic manufacturers of precursor cathode active materials (pCAM) and cathode active materials (CAM). These materials are used in battery production, and the lack of domestic manufacturing limits the market for recovered metals.
"Recycling, refining and cell manufacturing need to grow together, backed by consistent EPR enforcement and clear standards for grading black mass," Daphal said.
Nitin Gupta, co-founder and chief executive officer (CEO) at critical mineral and recycling firm Attero, told Business Standard that the need to develop domestic critical mineral processing capabilities should be viewed as a strategic priority rather than simply a question of industry challenges.
He said China controls a significant share -- 70 to 99 per cent -- of the global critical mineral supply chain and has used its position in trade negotiations. "China has increasingly used its control over critical minerals as a tool of economic warfare over the past couple of years. It has threatened to ban exports of these minerals to India, the US and Europe," he added.
Gupta said countries were now investing in developing their own processing capabilities to reduce such risks. He cited spending by the US and Europe, along with India's National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM).
The mission provides capital expenditure support for setting up refining facilities to process materials recovered from electronic waste, lithium-ion batteries and other sources of critical minerals such as nickel, cobalt and lithium, he said.
"So, I don't think this is about the challenges. It is something that needs to be done," he said.
What the ban means for India's EV ambitions
The export restriction could also support India's efforts to develop a domestic battery manufacturing ecosystem, particularly by making more recovered materials available to cell manufacturers.
Daphal said retaining battery scrap within the country could help strengthen the link between recycling and battery production. "Recovered lithium, nickel and cobalt can then go back into Indian cell manufacturing, which reduces how much the EV industry depends on imported minerals and on supply from China," he said.
He added that the move was also relevant to the recycled-content requirements under India's Battery Waste Management Rules. From FY28 onwards, battery producers will have to use minimum quantities of domestically recycled materials in new batteries. However, the restriction could have some near-term implications.
"In the short term, recyclers that only produce black mass may see lower prices, since they lose access to export buyers."
Daphal said the short-term adjustment could be necessary to encourage investment in domestic processing capabilities. He added that the extent of the benefits would depend on how effectively Customs authorities enforced the export restriction.
Gupta also said the move could help address an earlier gap in India's battery manufacturing plans. He cited the Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage scheme, under which the government had sought to develop 50 gigawatt-hours of domestic battery cell manufacturing capacity. The scheme, he said, did not achieve its intended outcome because of the lack of domestically available materials.
"Now, this ban on black mass exports will help develop India's domestic refining capabilities, which, in turn, will benefit the EV industry," he said.

Nvidia (NVDA) CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO after Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of an affair with a Chinese spy and a company executive.
Kress, one of Nvidia's more prominent executives, joined the company in 2013 and helped guide its financial success, transforming it from a video game company into the AI juggernaut it is today.
In a statement, Kress said she is committed to building on the work Jensen has done to turn Nvidia into the company it has become.
"We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," she said.
Kress regularly provides financial updates during Nvidia's quarterly earnings call, making her well-known among analysts and investors.
Prior to joining the company, Kress served as senior vice president and CFO for Cisco's (CSCO) Business Technology and Operations Finance group, according to her Nvidia biography.
Before joining Cisco, she held positions at Microsoft (MSFT) for 13 years, including as CFO of the company's Server and Tools group. She also worked at Texas Instruments (TXN) in several roles.
"Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position," newly appointed Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.
"She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia's strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," he added.
Kress succeeds Huang, who is embroiled in two alleged affairs: one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell.
On Sunday, Huang issued a statement admitting to the initial affair, apologizing to his family and Nvidia employees.
According to reports, the woman Huang was seeing, Alice Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based technology firm MegaSpeed and was allegedly acting as a spy on behalf of the Chinese government.
Nvidia's board has said it has launched an independent investigation into the matter, but added it has no reason to believe Nvidia trade secrets or national security were compromised.

india-b8ff9020ff.headline: India's exports up 29.9% in October; trade deficit narrows to $20.09 billion
india-b8ff9020ff.fulltext:
India’s merchandise exports rose to an all-time high of $49.5 billion in October 2026, bringing down the country’s overall trade deficit, official data released on Friday showed.
While a large part of this growth was due to petroleum products, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said diversification of exports to various locations helped improve the numbers.
India’s total exports, including goods and services, stood at $89.99 billion in October 2026, up nearly 30% from last October.
The overall trade deficit shrank from $25.1 billion last October to $20.1 billion year-on-year.
Goods trade leads the way
“In the month of October, the exports of merchandise exports have registered a new peak of $49.47 billion,” Mr. Agrawal said at a press briefing. “This is the highest-ever monthly merchandise export value, along with the highest monthly growth of 45.03% in the last five years.”
Merchandise imports rose to a record high of $89.35 billion in October 2026, up 16.5% YoY. Total imports stood at $110.1 billion, a 16.6% increase.
According to trade experts, goods exports growing faster than merchandise imports shows that while the rise in global prices contributed to the increase in the value of India’s exports, there was also an increase in the underlying export volumes.
Diversification strategy working
“The particularly encouraging part of this growth is that this is not in any particular sector, this is not in any particular geography, it is broad-based across countries and regions,” Mr. Agrawal added. “43 of our 50 top export destinations posted positive growth in October 2026 as compared to 2025.”
The data show that India’s exports to 12 out of its top 20 export destinations grew by double digits or more.
Mr. Agrawal pointed out that India’s exports to its free trade agreement (FTA) partners had grown strongly.
One of the key areas of diversification has been the African continent, with exports to that region growing 44% in April-September 2026 to $31.4 billion.
Trade with West Asia recovering
Notably, India’s trade with West Asia is recovering as countries find alternate routes and ports other than those along the constrained Strait of Hormuz.
India’s exports to West Asia increased to $5.7 billion in October 2026, compared to $5.5 billion YoY. Imports from the region stood at $16.2 billion versus $15.99 billion during the period.
In previous briefings, Mr. Agrawal had said that some new ports in the region were becoming more operational and were handling more cargo. These included some ports in Oman that are outside the Strait of Hormuz and the Fujairah and Khor Fakkan ports in UAE.
Services trade remains strong
India’s services trade remained robust in October 2026. Services exports grew to $40.5 billion as compared to $35.2 billion in October last year — a 15% growth.
Services imports grew to $20.7 billion from $17.7 billion over the same period, a 17% increase.
The final services export figure for October, however, will be made available only next month once the Reserve Bank of India releases its figures.

health-tech-7d5048ffba.headline: Pharmaceutical ads may influence which drug AI recommends, new research finds
health-tech-7d5048ffba.fulltext:
A study published in The Lancet Digital Health comes as more patients and physicians are looking to chatbots for treatment options.
Next time you ask AI for medical advice, you may want to consider whether it’s been influenced by Big Pharma. Prescription drug advertisements are everywhere and may affect AI’s recommendations, according to a study published in The Lancet Digital Health this week.
The study authors conducted experiments with a dozen consumer-facing large language models (LLMs), including versions of Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT—made by Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, respectively.
The models were tested across 33 scenarios that each included a clinical case description and multiple treatment options. In some cases, the AI models were also given an ad for one of the treatment options. The ad’s content included information about the drug and its uses, but did not specifically direct the AI model to recommend the drug.
When exposed to an ad, AI models recommended the treatment in question an average of 47.6% of the time, compared with 35% when no ad was present. However, the size of these shifts varied among the 12 models.
Although the models often changed their recommendation when an ad was present, in most cases they still selected one of the appropriate options. The outputs only disclosed the ad’s presence about 30% of the time.
“An answer can be clinically reasonable and still raise an important question about why the AI arrived at that answer,” study author Dr. Girish Nadkarni, a professor of medicine and system chair of the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai’s Icahn School of Medicine, said in a statement. “As AI becomes part of how people get health information, we need to be able to distinguish clinical guidance from commercial influence and be transparent about when advertising is part of the interaction.”
Pharmaceutical companies spent more than $6 billion on TV advertising alone in 2024, according to a report by the pharmaceutical data, analytics, and consulting firm IQVIA, which said that direct-to-consumer advertising “directly influences patient requests and prescription rates, driving real action in healthcare.”
All high-income countries, save for the U.S. and New Zealand, ban direct-to-consumer ads for prescription drugs.
In the U.S., prescription drugs consume more than 30% of commercial time during major networks’ evening news programs, according to a 2025 press release from the U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

other-interests-ddf94a746f.headline: AI confirms a long-suspected limit on quantum computers’ advantages
other-interests-ddf94a746f.fulltext:
A decades-old, vastly influential conjecture about quantum computing has finally been proven – by AI. It confirms that a whole class of mathematical problems wouldn’t be more easily solved by quantum computers.
In 1999, Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin got stuck on a question about when exactly quantum computers could excel over their conventional counterparts.
At this time, researchers knew of at least one example of a problem where the quantum approach outshone all others: Shor’s algorithm for factoring numbers. But they suspected that this hinged on the specific mathematical structure that underlies the factoring problem.
Advertisement
Aaronson wondered whether quantum computers could also win in the opposite case, when the problem contains little to no structure and lots of randomness instead. In 2011, he and Andris Ambainis at the University of Latvia formally conjectured that, in at least one case, the answer was negative – but they couldn’t prove it.
Now, David Turturean at the start-up Physical Superintelligence (PSI) and his colleagues have used Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to provide that proof. This eliminates a whole class of problems from the race to understand what quantum computers are best at.
“It’s a very crisp mathematical question that has consequences for quantum computing, and it has been very hard to solve, to the degree that I had given up on it my myself,” says Ambainis.
“This might be one of the [few] remaining long-standing open questions that are worth pursuing,” says Turturean.
The problem at the heart of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture requires a computer to answer a “yes” or “no” question after being fed a huge but random string of bits, or 1s and 0s. Could a quantum computer get an answer by looking at the string significantly fewer times than a conventional computer would have to? The pair conjectured that a conventional computer could approximate the quantum computer’s performance for most strings and without having to take much longer. More simply, you could get away with not using a quantum computer at all.
Importantly, Aaronson and Ambainis translated the statement at the core of their conjecture into the language of polynomials, recasting it as a problem in a different field of pure mathematics. “We didn’t think it would catch on like it did. People who were powerhouses in their own fields and didn’t care about quantum computing got interested,” says Aaronson.
PSI’s breakthrough builds on the work of such mathematicians. Turturean says it took about four days for Fable 5.2, which wasn’t publicly available at the time, to complete the proof, improve and refine it twice, then verify the final version with the proof-checking software Lean. The PSI team then shared the proof with Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan at Stanford University in California, who studied it and wrote an exposition that unravelled its key ingredients.
In a joint statement to New Scientist, they wrote that the new proof meaningfully surpasses all studies that it draws upon. “The proofs are entirely different – and substantially more difficult. Everything is also woven together in a novel way,” they wrote.
Three days after PSI made their proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture public, Supartha Podder at Stony Brook University in New York and his colleagues put forward another, shorter proof of the same thesis, developed with the aid of ChatGPT 5.6 and 6. After four months of building out the framework for their proof, one part of the work by Turturean and his colleagues “supplied the missing ingredient that allowed this approach to succeed”, the researchers wrote in their paper, which was only about seven pages long.
Shachar Lovett at the University of California, San Diego, whose work was one of the key ingredients in the PSI proof, says that this exposition reveals tricks that mathematicians can now learn from and reuse. “This helps us guide our research. What I think is going to come from these AI tools is that now we can maybe ask more ambitious questions,” he says.
But Lovett is cautious about the impact this new work might have on quantum computing, as it is more mathematical than practical, he says. In Aaronson’s view, the weight of the practical implications is also unclear. “This rules out a potential direction where you could look for quantum speed-ups, but it wasn’t a plausible direction anyway,” he says. The glaring question now is where to look for new problems that quantum computers are uniquely positioned to take on.
“This is far from the end of quantum speedups. Instead, it informs us on what types of problems we should consider,” wrote the Stanford team. A similar problem with a shorter or less random input string, or one for which the quantum computer doesn’t give just a “yes” or “no” answer, could still benefit from the quantum approach, they wrote. This leaves tremendously many problems, including simulating industrially relevant molecules and some optimisation problems.
Aaronson says that many of the questions related to quantum information science that are best tackled with mathematics have already been answered by AI, so it is time to formulate some new ones. Matthew Pines at PSI says he and his colleagues now also want to use AI to explore new ideas, instead of just knocking down famous problems. The future will show how successful this can be. “There is some major creative leap needed. I think that’s something where AI is not good yet,” says Ambainis.

work-careers-5ff5a6295c.headline: Microsoft’s massive outage puts its AI-driven layoffs under scrutiny
work-careers-5ff5a6295c.fulltext:
Microsoft’s massive service outage on Thursday left businesses and government agencies scrambling to access critical services. It also came at an awkward moment for the tech giant, which has undertaken an extensive initiative to reduce its workforce even as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence.
Recent efforts to trim the company’s head count included extending buyout offers to 9,000 U.S. employees in April and 60,000 employees in four countries in October. It also laid off 4,800 workers in July, mostly in its sales and Xbox divisions. Last month, The Information also reported that leadership in Microsoft’s Azure cloud division had discussed cutting costs by at least 20%; Microsoft denied the report.
Meanwhile, the company is pouring billions into AI infrastructure. Earlier this year, it projected roughly $190 billion in capital expenditures for 2026, much of it driven by the enormous computing demands of AI and cloud services.
Fast Company has reached out to Microsoft for comment.
There is no evidence that either the workforce reductions or AI investments directly contributed to Thursday’s disruption. But the incident raises a broader question for Microsoft and the tech industry: As businesses shrink their workforces and increasingly rely on AI to boost productivity, are they also risking the reliability of their existing products?
Workforce reductions and restructurings can push out experienced employees who understand how a company’s systems work, including any longtime bugs or quirks, and who know how to respond when something breaks. Even if layoffs don’t directly cause technical problems, the loss of institutional knowledge can make those problems harder to solve.
Enacting such reductions while also adapting to a rapidly changing technology like AI may be especially risky. As companies reorganize around these new tools, fewer resources may be available to maintain and troubleshoot existing systems.
