longform-bab44f79de.headline: Silicon Valley’s Chaos Moment
longform-bab44f79de.fulltext:
As the Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has fallen this week—shaking the American economy, which AI helps hold together—Anthropic prepares for an IPO at an expected valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. In this episode, Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel talks about Huang’s resignation, and the danger of having such a figure bear the weight of the economy. Then he talks to the Vox reporter Sigal Samuel about Anthropic’s IPO, how the AI race has influenced the company’s ideology, and why it and other companies refuse to slow down or stop.
Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain. We’ve got a great episode for you today where we talk to Vox reporter Sigal Samuel about the AI race and Anthropic’s upcoming IPO.
But first, there is very big news that I need to address. On Thursday morning, Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia and arguably the most important figure in the world of artificial intelligence, resigned from the company. This is a shocking development that just one week ago seemed utterly impossible.
Huang’s resignation came after reports that he was engaged in an extramarital affair with a businesswoman who, turns out, was an asset for Chinese intelligence. Huang admitted to the relationship, Silicon Valley circled the wagons to defend him, while many in Congress demanded investigations into Huang, Nvidia, and its relationship to China.
And the logic for keeping him in place was very simple. Huang is seen as the visionary of the AI boom—a man who, more than a decade before generative AI, made this bet that his graphics-processor company could be used to train neural networks and artificial intelligence. It was an unpopular decision, but Huang held course. He was patient, and over time the bet paid off.
Nvidia became the company that built the chips that would train and help power AI data centers and models. As The New Yorker’s Stephen Witt wrote in a 2023 profile of Huang, “The revelation that ChatGPT … had been trained on an Nvidia supercomputer spurred one of the largest single-day gains in stock-market history.”
And Nvidia became this juggernaut: one of the most valuable companies of all time. Just last month, Nvidia’s valuation hit $5.7 trillion, which is larger than every economy except the United States and China. And some estimates suggest that Nvidia provided 90 percent of the advanced chips used in the AI industry. And Huang used Nvidia’s endless profits to become arguably the lead investor in the artificial-intelligence boom. He famously saw the industry as this five-layer cake of components, and he pledged to distribute Nvidia’s money and technology across every layer of it.
The company, as of July, had invested $99 billion into AI companies—including OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX, and data-center providers like CoreWeave. He pioneered this circular style of investment, where companies pay Nvidia for the chips, and then Nvidia puts that money back into the companies, in part so they can keep buying chips. Now, some saw this as genius, right? The Bank of Nvidia. And others saw this as the beginnings of what could turn into a disastrous bubble.
But regardless, Huang—who brokered many of these deals himself—and Nvidia, they both affixed themselves as this load-bearing beam of the AI boom. Huang seemed invincible, unflappable. And Nvidia’s success wasn’t just guaranteed; it was necessary to make sure that the music didn’t stop, causing the entire industry to crash down with it.
And so all of this is very important context for why Huang’s relationship with a Chinese asset, an individual who may have been using her relationship to Huang to help get chips into China via export loopholes, why that didn’t immediately sink Huang. Many, like The Economist, called for his resignation. This wasn’t just a national-security issue; this was an affair with an Nvidia client. But in some cases, Nvidia was just believed as too big to fail. And Huang, who is the leader, with no clear successor, was needed to ensure that the AI boom could move onward, so that the numbers could keep going up.
On Wednesday, news broke in the Times that Huang had had a second affair, this time with an Nvidia employee who was a direct report. And what was framed by some defenders earlier as just a slip-up, or this human dalliance, it became a pattern. A display of real recklessness, and a sign that the indiscretions of the company’s leader was too much to bear. So on Thursday, Huang resigned.
Colette Cress, who is Nvidia’s chief financial officer, will serve as interim CEO. But this is—make no mistakes—unprecedented territory. Earlier this week on an episode of Radio Atlantic, I was asked what the nightmare scenario would be: not just for Nvidia, but for the economy in general. And I said that it would be that Jensen Huang was no longer the CEO of Nvidia.
Because Jensen Huang isn’t just somebody who is a big part of this company or helped found it. He’s the central node. He is the person who allocates where all of the chips go. He has become an adviser to Donald Trump, to all sorts of people inside the AI industry. He’s basically the person who, if you try to imagine the industry without him, you don’t really know what any of it looks like. Dan Ives, who’s a financial analyst, said this week that Nvidia would be worth 25 percent to 30 percent less without Jensen Huang, which is a crazy figure to think about.
What happens if Nvidia’s stock plunges? If Nvidia can’t make up its investments that it’s already promised to different people? What if people who have investments through Nvidia, who buy chips from Nvidia, decide all of a sudden that they don’t want to do so? Because Huang is the person whom they trusted and whose leadership they expected to have steward the company through the next 10 to 15 years?
I think an obvious question here is: Why is Jensen Huang so important? Why couldn’t Nvidia just go on without him? And in some sense, they will. They will continue to keep making chips. People will continue to buy those chips. But Huang wasn’t just a person who had a good vision at some point. Huang was also somebody who brokered a lot of these deals himself. He was the person who projected the confidence of the industry.
And in a lot of ways, Huang is sort of the adult in the room in the AI industry. Huang’s not an AI doomer. He’s someone who forcibly comes out and says, These are technological problems, and we’re going to solve them like adults. He is not only an anchor in terms of the relationships that he has with everyone from Donald Trump to every single AI CEO in the industry. He’s also somebody whose unshakable confidence was very key to continuing to invest and feel good about the trajectory of the AI industry.
Thinking about this for the last couple hours after Huang resigned, I had a few general thoughts. I think, first: This is arguably what happens when you have a person who’s just become larger than life. The AI boom, and Silicon Valley in general, likes to canonize its CEOs—to make them these big, huge, load-bearing figures. And in some cases, that’s good, right? It’s good for the company’s story; it’s good for the stock. It’s good for those figures themselves, while things are going well.
But it leads to moments like this, where—when that person is no longer at the helm of the company, or when they have to step down, or if something happens to them—you open yourself up to all of these risks. And you open the market and the global economy up to all of these risks. And it seems like, in this moment, maybe it’s not such a good idea that we turn these businessmen, these flawed individuals, into load-bearing figures of the economy. And honestly, that may be the biggest risk and vulnerability of all in this.
I think that Jensen Huang has proven to be more of a pragmatic guy, right? He is not an AI doomer. But still, there is this really big disconnect that I see here, between the AI leaders and tech CEOs who are talking about this historic responsibility of artificial intelligence, this unprecedented money. This technology that’s going to remake the world, get rid of all sorts of jobs, potentially cause the end of human civilization. They’re building God and human consciousness.
And yet, these people do not always seem to behave like serious people. Like people who are in charge of this. They’re taking very big risks. And it’s not clear that they understand their own logic, that they are in charge of something so important. ’Cause if they were, maybe they wouldn’t be doing things like having these affairs.
I’ve been thinking about Huang as somebody who has made this huge, long, patient bet on pivoting to AI. It’s arguably the greatest bet in the history of technology. And he held on while it was deeply unpopular to do so. And when it paid off, he became this rock star: this amazing, crucial figure. He became one of the richest people in the world. His company, which made computer-graphics cards, turned into something that was going to usher in the next industrial revolution.
And so he’s used to shouldering this unbelievable amount of risk. He’s used to doing what he wants, even if it’s risky, and having it pay off. And I think we can’t divorce that mindset from the behavior that we’ve seen that’s allowed him to have to step down. Maybe now this is the first time that he’s taken a risky situation. He’s done what he wanted to do, but this time it backfired.
Still, what’s really interesting about this moment is how many people are still out there in Silicon Valley defending Huang. Who are saying that this was just an indiscretion, that Huang is still the visionary who he was, that the American economy and the AI industry and Nvidia all need him, and that he shouldn’t be forced to step down because of some flawed decisions that he’s made.
It’s part of what I’ve been thinking of through this whole scandal as the flawed logic of the AI boom, right?
This scandal had a very befitting irony for the AI moment, where Huang seemingly cozied up to his industry’s No. 1 foe, in China—which is the boogeyman that has made Silicon Valley executives say that they have to build this technology that they fear, right? In order not to lose to China. But instead of denouncing him, Silicon Valley is motivated to circle the wagons. Because doing so keeps the system moving, keeps progress going, keeps money flowing. So that the AI industry can beat China, right?
It’s a pretzel style of logic. And that I think is the type of warped incentive that the AI race produces. Playing this game means that you have to shoulder this ridiculous amount of risk. And you have to make compromises or use logic. That doesn’t always make sense. And what ends up happening is: You start to behave in ways that don’t make sense to people who aren’t running the race, who aren’t inside the boom.
And so I think what we’re seeing now are a bunch of people trying to deal with that warped logic. Trying to understand what to do now that they’ve yoked themselves not only to this company, but to this man—and that the future of their industry now seems very uncertain with his removal.
After the break, we’re going to explore more of that Silicon Valley flawed logic with my guest, Sigal Samuel.
Warzel: For the last year or so, but especially for the last few months, I’ve been stuck on the logic of the AI boom.
This is an industry that frequently invokes the language of existential doom. And it seems both energized by, but also deeply disturbed by, what it’s building. This is an industry that has some of its safety advocates saying things like, If anyone builds it, everyone dies.
And yet, they are building. Despite alarming, unexpected behavior from the models. indian-startups-cac1e20ff3.headline: MeitY examines data collection by home services platforms for physical AI training
indian-startups-cac1e20ff3.fulltext:
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has raised concerns over the collection of first-person video and sensor data from gig workers to train physical AI models. The scrutiny comes amid Pronto’s in-home video recording initiative, while rival platforms Snabbit and Urban Company have decided against adopting the practice.
According to an ET report, senior officials from the ministry met representatives of home services platforms, including Snabbit, Pronto and Urban Company, along with technology and robotics companies on Thursday to discuss concerns around workers’ rights, consumer privacy and data sovereignty.
The meeting, chaired by MeitY secretary S Krishnan, sought details on standard operating procedures (SOPs) for collecting, processing and storing first-person video recordings. The ministry also asked companies about safeguards to obtain workers’ consent and protect the privacy of household members and other individuals captured in the footage.
Companies were also questioned on whether the data collected was being sold, shared or transferred to AI developers outside India. The ministry sought disclosures on data-sharing agreements, vendor contracts, retention policies and the nature and scale of information being collected.
Among the three home services platforms, Pronto has started in-home video recording through its Verified service. Snabbit and Urban Company have ruled out adopting the practice. According to ET, Pronto has been asked to submit a detailed representation on its data collection practices and SOPs.
Some executives at the meeting also raised concerns about collecting data in India and selling it to overseas physical AI developers, arguing that the practice does not put the country in a favourable position. Robotics startups also suggested that India should focus on developing domestic physical AI capabilities rather than supplying training data to overseas companies.
In a statement, Pronto said it participated in the MeitY consultation as part of a broader industry discussion on responsible data practices. The company said data generated through its customer booking journey involves customer consent and can support downstream AI applications. It added that its existing practices are designed to comply with applicable regulations and that it would continue to engage with the ministry as the policy framework evolves.
Pronto’s data collection initiative comes months after the Bengaluru-based startup raised $20 million from US-based tech investor Lachy Groom, co-founder of AI startup Physical Intelligence. Its founder, Anjali Sardana, has also set up a new physical AI venture, Provision Labs, which works with developers building AI models for robotics and other real-world applications.
Investor interest in India’s physical AI ecosystem has also grown. According to an Entrackr report, startups in the segment raised around $155 million across 31 deals as of July 2026, compared with $130 million across 25 deals in 2025.
A separate set of companies is building the data collection, annotation and training infrastructure required for physical AI systems. Human Archive is developing human sensorimotor datasets for robots, while Neo Cambrian has launched an India-focused robotics data factory. Other companies operating across this segment in India include iMerit, Human Stryde, Luel, Awign, Build, Centific, Humyn Labs, Aura ML, Build AI, FPV Labs and Northstar.
Physical AI models require real-world data that captures human actions, objects, environments and interactions. Much of this data has to be collected specifically for robotics and embodied AI use cases rather than sourced from existing internet datasets.
ET also quoted legal experts highlighting that video recordings, facial images, location traces and sensor data could qualify as personal data when they identify or can reasonably be linked to a worker. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act requires platforms to provide clear notices on data collection and processing purposes, worker rights and grievance mechanisms.
The development follows earlier discussions among startups working on physical AI to establish common standards for worker pay, wellbeing, working hours, safety and legal compliance.

Microsoft is struggling to restore its workplace services following a global outage that disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and several other Microsoft 365 applications, affecting businesses, financial institutions, airlines and government operations across multiple countries.
The disruption, which began on Thursday continued into Friday with Microsoft's initial recovery measures failing to deliver sustained improvements. The company is now exploring alternative ways to restore infrastructure capacity and stabilise its services, Microsoft said in a statement.
Here is what happened, how the outage affected users and businesses, and when Microsoft expects services to return to normal.
Quick answers to key questions
•5 QUESTIONS
1
What caused the Microsoft outage?⌵
Microsoft said a core process on affected servers became overwhelmed, causing servers to stop responding and reducing available infrastructure capacity. The loss of server availability shifted more workloads onto the remaining systems, adding pressure.
2
Which Microsoft services were affected by the outage?⌵
The disruption affected services connected to Exchange Online, including Outlook, Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot. SharePoint, Planner, To Do, Microsoft Defender and some administrative and security tools were also affected.
3
How did the Microsoft outage affect businesses and financial firms?⌵
Financial institutions and trading desks reported communication problems, delayed financing transactions and backed-up trade confirmations. Some staff relied on phone calls, WhatsApp or fax, while airlines reported email and customer-support disruptions.
4
When will Microsoft services be fully restored?⌵
Microsoft has not announced a confirmed timeline for full restoration. It said its initial recovery measures did not deliver sustained improvements and that it was exploring other ways to increase capacity and stabilise services.
5
How can users check the status of the Microsoft outage?⌵
Users can monitor Microsoft's official service-health dashboard. The incident references provided by Microsoft are EX1550543 and MO1550821.
Microsoft's investigation found that a core process running on affected servers was becoming overwhelmed, causing the machines to stop responding and reducing available infrastructure capacity.
The unexpected unavailability of several servers shifted additional workloads onto the remaining infrastructure, creating further pressure on Microsoft's systems.
The disruption affected services connected to Exchange Online and email infrastructure, including Outlook, Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Other affected products and functions included SharePoint, Microsoft Defender, Planner, To Do and certain administrative and security tools.
Microsoft also reported difficulties with traffic routing between backend servers, adding to the challenge of restoring normal operations.
According to a Bloomberg report, financial institutions and trading desks across Asia faced communication difficulties. Traders at UBS, CMC Markets and other financial firms resorted to phone calls, WhatsApp and even fax machines to communicate with clients and colleagues. Some financing transactions were delayed, while trade confirmations backed up, creating settlement difficulties for back-office teams.
In Japan, the Finance Ministry reported that it could not receive emails for much of the day, Associated Press reported. New Zealand immigration authorities paused visa application processing, while some government departments and educational institutions warned of limited communication.
Indian airlines also reported disruptions to customer support. Air India temporarily rerouted its email services, although it said flight operations remained unaffected. IndiGo reported problems with email support, while Akasa Air warned passengers of delays in email responses. Delhi Airport also advised passengers to check their flight status before travelling.
According to Bloomberg, Downdetector received around 200,000 reports of problems across Microsoft services. Outlook-related complaints peaked at 138,058 on Thursday, before declining later in the day.

The company initially attempted to restart affected infrastructure, redirect traffic away from malfunctioning servers and redistribute workloads. It also introduced network and traffic-management changes to improve service availability.
However, these measures did not produce the expected results.
In its latest update on November 13, Microsoft said it had monitored the changes introduced to improve serviceability but found that they were not working as expected.
"We're identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances," the company said.
Microsoft is also working to increase server capacity and address machines that remain in an unstable state.
Microsoft has not announced a confirmed timeline for the complete restoration of its affected services.
Although some regions and functions have experienced partial recovery, the company has acknowledged that its recovery efforts have not yet delivered sustained improvements.

Microsoft Outlook went dark on Rita Elkazzi just as a volatile week in markets was coming to an end. As swings in AI stocks and bonds kept traders on edge, the UBS Group AG execution-sales head for Australia and New Zealand was forced onto phones and alternative channels to communicate.
“It’s been a bit of a disaster and I can’t believe still not resolved,” said Sydney-based Elkazzi. “It means a lot more diligence on ensuring trade recaps et cetera are accurate.”
Elkazzi’s experience is echoed by many after Microsoft Corp. suffered one of its most severe disruptions in recent memory. The tech giant is still struggling to restore access to some of its flagship software hours after an outage began, affecting its Outlook, Teams and Copilot systems. The difficulties in communicating efficiently have hindered workflows on trading desks, delayed corporate disclosure and even affected email access for Japan’s Ministry of Finance.
In Singapore, traders reported some banks’ inability to complete financing deals. Meanwhile, a few Indian brokerages sent out alerts to the potential impact on their services, with IIFL Capital Services informing their clients that there could be a delay in responding to emailed queries.
Australia’s main exchange operator ASX Ltd. told customers it’s aware of an issue affecting some Microsoft 365 services including email, adding that the bourse’s services remain available for normal operation. Workhorse Group Inc., a US truck and bus manufacturer, said it would postpone its earnings release.
In Japan, the government’s shared IT platform also experienced disruptions, with the finance ministry saying it can’t receive emails due to the outage.
Among those affected is Calvin Yeoh. The portfolio manager at hedge fund Blue Edge Advisors said he can’t check emails and is struggling to access brokerage reports and some trading platforms that require email authentication.
“Outlook is the appendix of the modern financial operations world,” said Yeoh. “So aside from the entire front to back infrastructure of global finance being crippled, and with Nvidia melting down and rates markets going wild this week, yeah it’s been all good.”
Meanwhile, CMC Markets traders are resorting to “old-school” trading as Microsoft’s systems went offline.
“Everyone was back on the phone, and our WhatsApp chats were busier than usual,” said Eugene Koh, sales trader at CMC Markets Singapore. “Something that normally takes a second on email might now take a phone call and a few minutes to get through.”

The outage has attracted about 200,000 reports of user issues across Microsoft services on Downdetector, ranking among the company’s most severe. Previous disruptions have rarely lasted more than several hours. Microsoft shares were down 0.4% in extended trading.
After initially struggling to identify the issue and test potential remedies, the company said in an update that it’s “seeing positive results with our efforts to restart affected infrastructure.”
Matthew Haupt, a portfolio manager at Wilson Asset Management, said the firm’s small cap team told him that some trading volumes in equities have fallen on the back of the blackout.
The outage has also left Kenneth Goh, who is travelling for work in Malaysia, unable to get market updates that help inform his advice to private clients, and it’s made worse during a volatile week of trading.
“It has been super irritating,” said Goh, director of private wealth management at broker UOB Kay Hian, who is relying on patchy phone calls to speak with clients. “If the outage crosses 24 hours, then we’d be in the red zone.”

As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America.
The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues".
In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".
The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade.
"We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday.
Will emails affected by the outage ever arrive?
Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery".
In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away.
Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up".
The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email.
When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent.
Why has it taken so long to fix?
Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time.
Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues.
"What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said.
"The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs.
"One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in.
"You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit."
The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time".
He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal.
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.
"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.
In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."
How many people have been affected?
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed.
Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected.
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed.
In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected.
The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.
Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report.

ai-87f721b4f8.headline: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
ai-87f721b4f8.fulltext:
It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.
Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.
Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.
Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.
Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.
“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”
Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.
For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.
“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”
It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.
If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.
Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.
While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.
Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.
Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.
“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.
Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

ai-423adf6f81.headline: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its 'dots' AI agents to make purchases for users
ai-423adf6f81.fulltext:
OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.
The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.
OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.
"Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.
ChatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts.
Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kick-start a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents.
OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an "Instant Checkout" feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products.
Nayak said ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI's previous efforts, particularly around product discovery.
"We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they're really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint," she said.
ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old. The limited rollout is intentional, and the "right approach to make sure things are working," said Luke Gebb, executive vice president and global head of innovation at Amex.
OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter. With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to.
"It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there," Gebb told CNBC in an interview.
Merchants and vendors are still reckoning with the rise of personal AI agents, and some companies have opted to forgo them entirely. United Airlines said Wednesday that it will block agents from accessing its systems to book tickets, and Amazon prevents the agents from purchasing products on its platform.
OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition. The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance.
"It's going to take time for the ecosystem to build the right infrastructure to be able to make this experience really amazing and seamless across all of their sites," Nayak said. "Really, who we are speaking to here is the networks and the merchants."

world-dabb9c4229.headline: Nvidia scandal fallout widens as Trump's treasury secretary blames cabinet colleague
world-dabb9c4229.fulltext:
Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal
- Published
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.
Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.
Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.
Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.
"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.
There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external.
"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past.
In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media.

- How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions 
  - Published1 day ago
Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.
Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.
According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.
A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.
"Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

world-de06bec5ec.headline: Nvidia scandal: US treasury chief blames Lutnick’s commerce department over alleged lack of action
world-de06bec5ec.fulltext:
The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, is facing growing pressure over his apparent lack of action over the Nvidia spying scandal as other Trump administration officials publicly raise questions over his decisions.
Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by the company’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, after reports emerged of his multiple affairs, most importantly with Alice Huang (no relation), who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be fired, the Associated Press reported, after it emerged that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in the Trump administration.
Lutnick is now scheduled to testify before Congress next month, just days after the ousted Nvidia chief answers lawmakers’ questions on Capitol Hill.
Lutnick is also facing criticism for a delay by the commerce department in adding Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is associated with Alice Huang and has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in recent years, to Washington’s blacklist of companies that the US considers a risk to national security despite reported concerns within the administration.
Bessent has “for months” been in favor of putting Megaspeed on the blacklist – but Lutnick’s commerce department “has the pen”, Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he added in an interview with the network on Friday.
John Curtis, a Utah Republican senator, said that Lutnick’s reported delay on export controls regarding Megaspeed “raises the question of whether the commerce department is acting in the best interests of the American people”.
The Republican senator John Cornyn told the Financial Times that there needed to be “a thorough investigation and accountability for the outrageous circumvention of national security export controls”, adding: “Heads should roll.”
The Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said Jensen Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether US security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about his reported relationship with Alice Huang.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.
Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge. The president called him two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported.
On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”
The House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.
Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair, said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him, citing “recent reports [that] raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology”.
The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal-conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to his “profound” contributions to the company he cofounded.
Huang is reported to have had relationships with Alice Huang as well as an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, according to the New York Times, and another, unnamed employee, according to Reuters.
The House foreign affairs chair, Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Huang’s testimony.
The House speaker, Mike Johnson, said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China.
Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company important to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.
“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters at the US Capitol, adding that he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“
Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models.
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday.
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as Huang’s swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for more than three decades.
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo.
Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.

Senior White House officials are discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out amid a spy scandal surrounding Nvidia’s now-former CEO Jensen Huang, two people familiar with the situation said on Thursday.
A growing number of lawmakers criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China.
Criticism ‌of Lutnick’s actions predates Thursday’s resignation of Huang, who said he would step down as CEO of the leading AI chipmaker after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.
But the charge that Lutnick has not done enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China has emerged as the fallout of Jensen Huang’s actions grows.
The White House and Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment after Reuters reported White House officials were discussing Lutnick’s future. Earlier on Thursday, a White House official said US President Donald Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position”.
In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held off from adding China’s ⁠AI start-up DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to a trade blacklist.
The US has not posted any additions to that list since October 2025, ‌the longest stretch between new postings in more than a decade. Reuters earlier reported that the US Commerce Department has not added new Chinese companies to that list for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China.
“Secretary Howard Lutnick and undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not ‌closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fuelling China’s military,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, said.
Warren, who will chair ⁠the Senate Banking Committee starting in January, and ⁠incoming Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chair Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat, wrote to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, telling the administration to preserve all documents related to Nvidia’s exports of advanced AI ‌chips to China and related national security risks.
The senators cited reports of Jensen Huang’s personal relationship with Alice Huang, an executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought more than US$4.8 billion in advanced Nvidia AI chips since June 2024.
US Senator Ron ‌Wyden ‌of Oregon and Congressman Richard Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrats on the Senate Finance Committee and House Ways and Means Committee, respectively, wrote to Lutnick on Thursday, saying they were investigating the administration’s ‌approval of sales of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to Chinese companies “with concerning links to the Chinese government, military, and sanctioned entities”.
The lawmakers also questioned Trump’s decision to grant Nvidia permission to sell its ⁠advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales through a Commerce Department action, which they called “an unconstitutional export tax”.
Jensen Huang supported more exports ⁠to China, despite repeated calls from China hawks in both parties to crack down on Beijing’s access to the technology.
Congressman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, said Congress needs to investigate the Commerce Department’s role in how it approves chip exports, adding that he has confidence in Lutnick.
Senator John ‌Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, told Politico that Lutnick needs ‌to answer questions about approving advanced US chip sales to China.
Lutnick, a Wall Street veteran who served as co-chairman of Trump’s transition team, has been friends with the US president for three decades and was a guest in 2008 on The Apprentice, the reality television show Trump hosted.
Axios reported on Wednesday that Lutnick stalled Trump’s crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s chips to China.
The Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, US Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas, urged Lutnick on Thursday to bar CXMT from the US market and deny it access to American technologies.

Bengaluru-based Desible.ai, a startup building automation tools for banks, NBFCs (non-banking financial companies), and insurers, has raised Rs 32 crore in a round led by Prime Venture Partners. Existing investor Invention Engine also participated in the funding.
The company will use the fresh capital to strengthen its AI capabilities and compliance infrastructure, expand sales and marketing operations, and improve product development.
Founded in 2025 by Uttam Tiwari and Omkar Raikar, Desible.ai is building an AI-powered workflow orchestration platform that helps financial institutions automate customer engagement, servicing, collections, and compliance-related processes. The company started with voice-based automation and is expanding its platform to channels such as WhatsApp, SMS, and email.
The startup currently works with insurance providers and is talks with more than 40 BFSI institutions, the company said in a statement. Its platform supports over 25 workflows across functions such as revenue generation, risk and compliance, collections, underwriting, customer service, and claims. It says it handles more than 10 million customer engagements every month.
“Voice AI is our entry point, not our destination. We are building an outcome driven agentic workflow orchestration platform for BFSI enterprises. Starting with insurance, our goal is to help financial institutions automate customer, compliance, and operational workflows while maintaining the trust and regulatory standards the industry demands,” said cofounder and CEO Uttam Tiwari.
The startup's offering integrates with existing enterprise systems and uses predefined decision-making rules to ensure that customer consent, regulatory disclosures, and escalation procedures are followed.
“In regulated industries, AI that is right most of the time is not enough. Every Desible workflow runs on deterministic decisioning, so disclosures, consent, and escalations happen exactly as defined, every time, with every step auditable,” said CTO Omkar Raikar, who’s also a cofounder.
The platform is designed to support use cases including insurance renewals, collections, lead qualification, customer onboarding, claims intimation, and cross-selling.
“AI adoption in financial services won’t be driven by generic models alone. It will be driven by companies that deeply understand regulated workflows, customer engagement, and compliance. Varun Aggarwal of Invention Engine said the accelerator has worked closely with the founders to develop the product, validate the market, and secure their first customers.

indian-startups-a5ab0c2655.fulltext:
Jensen Huang resigns after 33 years at Nvidia
Nvidia has appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive officer. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, chief executive officer and board member with immediate effect, ending his 33-year tenure as the company’s chief executive, following a turbulent week.
Nvidia has appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive officer. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.
Kress said, “Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
Kress will retain the finance role while serving as interim CEO. She joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies including Cisco and Microsoft.
The board appointed former Synopsys chief executive and executive chairman Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair.
Jones said Kress understood the business and its customers. He added, “The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
On November 8, Huang apologised in a company-published message for being unfaithful to his wife and pledged to co-operate with an independent board inquiry into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
Reports say Huang had another extramarital affair with a senior executive of Nvidia, in addition to the relationship with a Chinese national Alice Huang, who was allegedly recruited as an intelligence asset by the Chinese government.
On November 10, independent directors appointed former acting US attorney Joon H. Kim and law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the inquiry. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company information had been compromised.
Nvidia faces a fast-growing, increasingly competitive AI-chip market. Founded in 1993 as a graphics-chip maker, it later adapted GPUs for parallel computing through software such as CUDA.
In its latest reported quarter, ended on July 26, it recorded revenue of $96.2 billion, including $89 billion from data centres. Its next results are due on November 17.

In a blitz of speeches and interviews this week, Federal Reserve officials locked in market expectations for an interest-rate hike in December and opened the prospect of the first back-to-back increases since 2023.
The case for higher rates was given new urgency Tuesday when the October consumer-price report showed inflation accelerated and broadened across everyday goods and services.
"Inflation is far too high," said New York Fed President John Williams, while Chicago Fed's Austan Goolsbee described the data as "borderline disturbing." Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said officials may need to hike "more rapidly" than she expected, while Fed Governor Christopher Waller went as far as warning that a 50-basis-points move may be needed next month.
"December is clearly locked and loaded for a 25-basis-point hike," said Olu Sonola, head of US economics at Fitch Ratings. "The real questions are how quickly the next hike follows and how many more will ultimately be needed."
About half of the 19 officials who sit on the Federal Open Market Committee, and about half who will vote at the December and January meetings, have spoken over the course of the week. On the last two questions, the signals were mixed.
They ranged from Waller's reference to an outsized move to the Cleveland Fed's Beth Hammack reiterating her preference for more frequent, smaller rises, and Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson favoring a gradual pace for increases.
There was more bad news on Friday when data showed wholesale prices, which feed into the Fed's preferred measure of inflation, climbed in October from a year earlier at their fastest pace since 2022. Transportation and warehousing costs jumped, adding to evidence of persistent price pressures throughout the economy.
"It now sounds like there's a worry to get ahead of the re-acceleration and increase the frequency and potentially increase what the FOMC views as terminal," meaning how high the rates should ultimately go, said Michael Reid, head of US economics at the Royal Bank of Canada.
Fed Call Changes
Economists at Bank of America and at Santander US Capital Markets increased the number of hikes they expect following the week of data and the flurry of speeches. Bank of America now sees increases at the next three Fed meetings, while Santander is projecting two raises, in December and March.

India's overall trade deficit narrowed to USD 20.09 billion in October 2026 from USD 25.15 billion in the corresponding month last year, as combined merchandise and services exports grew 29.9 per cent year-on-year to USD 89.99 billion.
Total imports, including merchandise and services, rose to USD 110.07 billion from USD 94.42 billion in October 2025.
The latest trade figures indicate an improvement in India's overall external trade balance, supported by stronger export growth. The narrow deficit comes even as the country's merchandise trade gap widened during the month.
Merchandise Trade Gap Widens
Merchandise exports increased 45.06 per cent year-on-year to USD 49.47 billion in October, while merchandise imports rose to USD 89.35 billion. This resulted in a merchandise trade deficit of USD 39.88 billion, compared with USD 34.43 billion in October last year.
The divergence between the merchandise and overall trade balances reflects the contribution of services exports to India's external trade position. Combined merchandise and services exports stood at USD 89.99 billion, while total imports amounted to USD 110.07 billion.
The services segment helped offset the wider merchandise trade gap, contributing to a narrow overall deficit. The latest figures underline the importance of services exports in India's external trade performance, alongside the movement in merchandise shipments and imports.
The October data follows a period of focus on export growth and India's efforts to diversify overseas markets amid global trade uncertainty.

india-7596cc49d1.headline: India's exports jump 29.9% to $89.99 billion in October; overall trade deficit narrows
india-7596cc49d1.fulltext:
India's overall exports, comprising merchandise and services, rose 29.9 per cent year-on-year to $89.99 billion in October 2026, compared with $69.27 billion a year earlier, driven by a sharp increase in goods shipments, according to data released by the ministry of commerce and industry on Friday.
Overall imports also increased, rising to $110.07 billion from $94.42 billion in October 2025. However, the overall trade deficit narrowed to $20.09 billion from $25.15 billion in the year-ago month, as export growth outpaced the rise in imports.
Merchandise exports surged 45.06% to $49.47 billion in October from $34.11 billion a year earlier. Trade Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said India recorded its highest-ever monthly goods exports during the month, as quoted by Reuters.
However, the sharp rise in goods shipments was accompanied by a widening merchandise trade gap. The goods trade deficit climbed to $39.88 billion in October, its highest level in a year, according to a Reuters calculation based on government data. This was higher than the $30.21 billion deficit recorded in September and the $32.25 billion forecast by economists in a Reuters poll.
Merchandise imports rose to $89.35 billion in October from $76.69 billion in the corresponding month last year. 
Compared with September, exports increased from $44.40 billion, while imports rose from $74.61 billion.
In the services sector, exports were estimated at $40.51 billion in October, up from $35.17 billion a year earlier. Services imports also increased to an estimated $20.72 billion from $17.73 billion.
The services surplus helped offset the merchandise trade deficit, contributing to the narrowing of the overall trade gap. The ministry clarified that October services figures are estimates, as the latest actual data released by the Reserve Bank of India pertains to September.
India, the world's third-largest oil consumer, imports nearly 85 per cent of its crude oil requirements. Higher import costs amid disruptions in global energy markets following the Middle East conflict have added pressure to its trade balance. A fall in Brent crude prices to around $92 a barrel has offered some relief.
India's export performance has also been supported by efforts to diversify markets and expand trade ties. New Delhi has implemented trade agreements with the UK and New Zealand this year, while a trade deal with the European Union is expected to be implemented early next year.

global-economics-c1f4667f7b.headline: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
global-economics-c1f4667f7b.fulltext:
Threats from artificial intelligence topped the list for greatest risks to the financial system, far exceeding any other dangers, according to respondents who participated in a Federal Reserve survey released Friday.
The central bank's twice-yearly look at a variety of dangers saw a surge in respondents saying that the biggest danger comes from AI along several fronts including debt, stock market valuations and security risks.
"Respondents noted three distinct areas of concern: (1) elevated equity valuations and the possibility that lower-than-expected earnings could result in lower valuations and a market correction; (2) cybersecurity risk, stemming from either a malicious attack by sophisticated state actors or damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and (3) risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing," the report stated.
The report comes with Wall Street on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, while communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers used to power the technology. Some 56% of voters in this month's midterm elections said data centers were of crucial or major importance in their choices, according to exit polling.
Respondents to the Fed survey released Friday include a variety of market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources. The report covers the period up to Oct. 28, just a few days shy of the election.
Of the group, 87% cited AI as a "salient risk" to the system. That was up from 50% in the survey during the spring of this year and well ahead of the next most-cited danger, a risk asset correction, which was mentioned by 52% of those surveyed.
Other leading risks were higher long-term rates (48%), cyberattacks (43%) and fiscal debt sustainability (43%), the latter coming with the U.S. debt over $40 trillion and the budget deficit near $2 trillion.
The report otherwise found the system fairly stable, though it mentioned that hedge fund leverage is at its highest since 2013 and concentrated on a relatively small group.

     US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to voluntarily testify before the Senate Banking Committee over concerns surrounding export controls on Nvidia’s advanced semiconductor chips and the handling of an investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company allegedly linked to China, CNN reported.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told CNN.
A source familiar with the matter said that arrangements for the testimony were still being worked out.
Lutnick’s decision came after Republican Senator Tim Scott, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, requested that he appear before the panel as part of its oversight of national security concerns related to semiconductor exports.
Scott had written to both Lutnick and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, requesting their voluntary appearance at a public hearing. The senator asked Lutnick to testify on December 10, 2026, while Huang was requested to appear on December 3, 2026.
In his letter to Lutnick, Scott highlighted the Commerce Department’s responsibility for administering and enforcing export control regulations, stating that the secretary’s testimony would be important for the committee’s oversight.
“Given the Department of Commerce’s central role in issuing and enforcing export control regulations, your testimony before the Committee will be essential to our oversight of these efforts,” Scott wrote.
Scott also raised concerns over national security and the protection of sensitive American technology, saying in a post on X, “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology. I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee. The American people deserve answers.”
The controversy centres on Nvidia’s Singapore-based customer Megaspeed International and allegations that the company may have links to Chinese intelligence. Its executive, Alice Huang, who is alleged to have ties with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, has reportedly come under scrutiny over suspected connections with Chinese intelligence, according to US intelligence officials.
According to CBS News, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security launched an investigation in 2024 into whether Nvidia chips supplied to Megaspeed were being diverted to China in violation of US export restrictions.
The investigation was subsequently transferred to the US Department of Justice, The New York Times reported.
The handling of the investigation has also drawn scrutiny over the Commerce Department’s decision not to place Megaspeed on its Entity List, which identifies foreign companies and individuals considered national security or foreign policy threats. Inclusion on the list restricts their access to American technology and products.
According to CBS News, the department has not added any company to the list since October 2025.
Lutnick has also faced questions over his professional and personal connections with Chinese companies and his relationship with the former Nvidia CEO, with concerns being raised about whether these associations influenced the department’s oversight of advanced AI chip exports.
The issue has reportedly led to tensions within the Trump administration. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick last week over the Commerce Department’s failure to include Megaspeed on the Entity List, as reported by CNN, citing sources.
Meanwhile, Scott has indicated that the committee could take further action if Huang does not agree to testify voluntarily. In his letter to the Nvidia chief executive, the senator warned that the panel could use compulsory measures.
“Should you fail to appear before the Committee on a voluntary basis, the Committee is prepared to use all tools at our disposal, including subpoenas, to conduct this legitimate and necessary oversight,” Scott wrote.
The Senate Banking Committee’s proposed hearings are expected to examine the handling of semiconductor export controls, the investigation involving Megaspeed and potential national security implications surrounding the overseas movement of sensitive American technology.
